Okay, the application has one video question: tell us about a turning point. I'll be the admissions person. Ready?
Ready. Well, in 2018 I was working in TV in Brazil, and I made up my mind to study color grading in Seoul.
Why was it a turning point, and not just a trip?
I didn't speak Korean, so every class was taught in English. It took me out of my comfort zone every single day.
Was it hard at first?
Very. In the first week, I hardly said anything. My teacher told me that I understood much more than I said. That was a wake-up call.
And when you look back on it now?
I see it as a stepping stone. Those six months paid off: I've used English at work almost every day since then.
That's a great answer. You've come a long way since our first class. But they always ask about setbacks.
There were a few. I bounced back from most of them, and that's exactly why I'm applying now.
Looking back, that was a real turning point for me.

When I look back on my career, the real turning point was not a big success. It was a small disaster. I was twenty-four, and I was working as a backing singer on a TV show. One night, the lead singer lost her voice an hour before the live broadcast, and the producer asked me to sing her part. I said yes before I really made up my mind. It was by far the most frightening night of my life. I forgot a few words in the second verse, and the next day the show was criticized in two newspapers. That was a setback, of course. But a week later, a songwriter called me. She told me that my voice sounded honest, and she asked me to sing on her demo. That demo was my stepping stone. I used to think that a mistake was the end of the story. Now I tell my students that the important part is not how you fall. It is how you bounce back.

For six years, I edited sound for commercials. The money was good, and I was very comfortable. Too comfortable. Then a director I worked with said something that I still remember. He told me that my work was clean, but that it had no personality. That was my wake-up call. I made up my mind to study film sound, and I applied to a course in London. The course was taught by people who worked on real films, and I was the oldest student in the class. In the first month, I was much slower than the younger students, and I hardly understood their jokes. But I had a lot of experience, and very few of them did. Slowly, it paid off. Today I work on documentaries, and my work is nowhere near as clean as it used to be. It is a lot more interesting. If you have been comfortable for too long, that is a sign. It is probably time to get out of your comfort zone.
